Part VI: Numerical Methods for Solving Macroeconomic Models

kapitaali.com
April 14, 2026

Connects to: All preceding analytical results

When analytical solutions exist, we use them. The Solow model has a closed-form transition path; the log-utility Diamond OLG has an algebraic steady state; the scalar NK MSV solution is a single formula. But these are the exceptions. In medium-scale DSGE models with ten or more state variables, financial frictions, occasionally-binding constraints, and heterogeneous agents, closed-form solutions are impossible. Numerical methods are not a fallback — they are the primary tool.

This part covers the five fundamental numerical techniques that underlie every computational macroeconomics software package, from Dynare to QuantEcon. Chapter 22 develops root-finding: bisection, Newton–Raphson (with a proof of quadratic convergence), and quasi-Newton methods for finding DSGE steady states. Chapter 23 covers numerical integration — trapezoidal rules, Gaussian quadrature, and Monte Carlo — for the expected-utility integrals that appear in dynamic programming and option pricing. Chapter 24 develops numerical optimization, from gradient descent through BFGS, applied to the central bank’s optimal policy problem. Chapter 25 addresses linear system solution: LU decomposition, sparse matrix methods, and QR — the linear algebra backbone of the Kalman filter (Chapter 20), the DSGE solution (Chapter 28), and the Leontief model (Chapter 2). Chapter 26 synthesizes everything into Monte Carlo simulation of macroeconomic models: the Tauchen discretization, Markov chain simulation, bootstrap confidence bands, and the particle filter for nonlinear state-space models.

The mathematical depth of this part is intentionally applied: every algorithm is derived from first principles (not just stated), and every derivation connects to a specific step in the macroeconomic workflow. The reader who works through these five chapters will understand not just how to call a numerical solver but what it is doing inside — and when it will fail.

Chapter 22: Solving Nonlinear Equations¶

Newton–Raphson for Steady-State Calculations

“Newton’s method is the most important algorithm in numerical analysis. Everything else is a variation on it.”

Cross-reference: Principles Ch. 5.2 (Solow steady state as a root); Ch. 5.3 (RCK modified Golden Rule); Ch. 23 (Taylor rule fixed point) [P:Ch.5.2, P:Ch.5.3, P:Ch.23]

22.1 The Steady State as a Root-Finding Problem¶

Every dynamic model has a steady state — a fixed point of the system’s law of motion where all variables remain constant over time. Finding the steady state is the first step in any DSGE analysis: the log-linearization (Chapter 27) is performed around the steady state, and the Blanchard–Kahn solution (Chapter 28) requires knowing it precisely.

In simple models, steady states have closed-form solutions. The Solow model gives k~∗=(s/μ)1/(1−α)\tilde{k}^* = (s/\mu)^{1/(1-\alpha)}k~∗=(s/μ)1/(1−α); the log-utility Diamond OLG gives a direct algebraic expression. But in medium-scale DSGE models with multiple nonlinear equilibrium conditions — price-setting optimization, labor market search-and-matching, financial frictions — no closed form exists. We must solve a system of nonlinear equations:

F(x)=0,F:Rn→Rn.\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}, \quad \mathbf{F}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n.F(x)=0,F:Rn→Rn.
(1)

The methods of this chapter — bisection, Newton–Raphson, quasi-Newton — address this problem with different trade-offs between reliability and speed.

22.2 The Bisection Method¶

Algorithm 22.1 (Bisection).

Input: Continuous function f:R→Rf: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}f:R→R; bracket [a,b][a, b][a,b] with f(a)f(b)<0f(a)f(b) < 0f(a)f(b)<0; tolerance ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0.

  1. Set a0=aa_0 = aa0​=a, b0=bb_0 = bb0​=b.

  2. For n=0,1,2,…n = 0, 1, 2, \ldotsn=0,1,2,…:

    • mn=(an+bn)/2m_n = (a_n + b_n)/2mn​=(an​+bn​)/2 (midpoint).

    • If ∣bn−an∣<2ε|b_n - a_n| < 2\varepsilon∣bn​−an​∣<2ε or ∣f(mn)∣<ε|f(m_n)| < \varepsilon∣f(mn​)∣<ε: return mnm_nmn​.

    • If f(an)f(mn)<0f(a_n)f(m_n) < 0f(an​)f(mn​)<0: set an+1=ana_{n+1} = a_nan+1​=an​, bn+1=mnb_{n+1} = m_nbn+1​=mn​.

    • Else: set an+1=mna_{n+1} = m_nan+1​=mn​, bn+1=bnb_{n+1} = b_nbn+1​=bn​.

Theorem 22.1 (Bisection Convergence). The bisection method converges to a root x∗x^*x∗ with:

∣mn−x∗∣≤b−a2n+1.|m_n - x^*| \leq \frac{b-a}{2^{n+1}}.∣mn​−x∗∣≤2n+1b−a​.
(2)

The number of iterations to achieve tolerance ε\varepsilonε is n≥⌈log⁡2((b−a)/ε)⌉n \geq \lceil\log_2((b-a)/\varepsilon)\rceiln≥⌈log2​((b−a)/ε)⌉.

Proof. At each step the bracket [an,bn][a_n, b_n][an​,bn​] halves in length: bn−an=(b−a)/2nb_n - a_n = (b-a)/2^nbn​−an​=(b−a)/2n. The root x∗x^*x∗ lies in the bracket, so ∣mn−x∗∣≤(bn−an)/2=(b−a)/2n+1|m_n - x^*| \leq (b_n - a_n)/2 = (b-a)/2^{n+1}∣mn​−x∗∣≤(bn​−an​)/2=(b−a)/2n+1. □\square□

Convergence rate: The error halves at each step — linear convergence with rate 1/21/21/2. To gain one decimal digit of accuracy requires about log⁡2(10)≈3.3\log_2(10) \approx 3.3log2​(10)≈3.3 iterations. For 10-digit accuracy from a bracket of width 1: n≈3.3×10=33n \approx 3.3 \times 10 = 33n≈3.3×10=33 iterations. Bisection is slow but guaranteed to converge whenever a bracket exists.

When to use bisection: When the function is continuous but not differentiable; when a bracket is available but convergence of faster methods is uncertain; as a fallback when Newton–Raphson fails to converge.

22.3 Newton–Raphson for Scalar Equations¶

Newton–Raphson is the workhorse of root-finding. It exploits derivative information to converge far faster than bisection.

Algorithm 22.2 (Newton–Raphson, Scalar).

Input: Differentiable f:R→Rf: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}f:R→R; initial guess x0x_0x0​; tolerance ε\varepsilonε.

  1. For n=0,1,2,…n = 0, 1, 2, \ldotsn=0,1,2,…:

    • Compute xn+1=xn−f(xn)/f′(xn)x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n)xn+1​=xn​−f(xn​)/f′(xn​).

    • If ∣xn+1−xn∣<ε|x_{n+1} - x_n| < \varepsilon∣xn+1​−xn​∣<ε: return xn+1x_{n+1}xn+1​.

Derivation from Taylor expansion. Expand fff around xnx_nxn​:

0=f(x∗)≈f(xn)+f′(xn)(x∗−xn)  ⟹  x∗≈xn−f(xn)f′(xn)≡xn+1.0 = f(x^*) \approx f(x_n) + f'(x_n)(x^* - x_n) \implies x^* \approx x_n - \frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)} \equiv x_{n+1}.0=f(x∗)≈f(xn​)+f′(xn​)(x∗−xn​)⟹x∗≈xn​−f′(xn​)f(xn​)​≡xn+1​.
(3)

The update xn+1=xn−f(xn)/f′(xn)x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n)xn+1​=xn​−f(xn​)/f′(xn​) is the xxx-intercept of the tangent line to fff at (xn,f(xn))(x_n, f(x_n))(xn​,f(xn​)). Geometrically, Newton–Raphson replaces the nonlinear fff with its linear approximation and solves that.

Theorem 22.2 (Quadratic Convergence of Newton–Raphson). Suppose fff is twice continuously differentiable, f(x∗)=0f(x^*) = 0f(x∗)=0, f′(x∗)≠0f'(x^*) \neq 0f′(x∗)=0, and the initial guess x0x_0x0​ is sufficiently close to x∗x^*x∗. Then:

∣xn+1−x∗∣≤C∣xn−x∗∣2,C=∣f′′(x∗)∣2∣f′(x∗)∣.|x_{n+1} - x^*| \leq C|x_n - x^*|^2, \quad C = \frac{|f''(x^*)|}{2|f'(x^*)|}.∣xn+1​−x∗∣≤C∣xn​−x∗∣2,C=2∣f′(x∗)∣∣f′′(x∗)∣​.
(4)

The error squares at each step — quadratic convergence. If ∣x0−x∗∣<10−1|x_0 - x^*| < 10^{-1}∣x0​−x∗∣<10−1, then after one step ∣x1−x∗∣≲C⋅10−2|x_1 - x^*| \lesssim C\cdot 10^{-2}∣x1​−x∗∣≲C⋅10−2; after two steps ∣x2−x∗∣≲C3⋅10−4|x_2 - x^*| \lesssim C^3 \cdot 10^{-4}∣x2​−x∗∣≲C3⋅10−4; after three steps ∣x3−x∗∣≲C7⋅10−8|x_3 - x^*| \lesssim C^7 \cdot 10^{-8}∣x3​−x∗∣≲C7⋅10−8. Three iterations from 1-digit accuracy gives 8-digit accuracy.

Proof. Let en=xn−x∗e_n = x_n - x^*en​=xn​−x∗. Taylor-expand f(xn)f(x_n)f(xn​) around x∗x^*x∗:

f(xn)=f(x∗)+f′(x∗)en+12f′′(ξn)en2=f′(x∗)en+12f′′(ξn)en2f(x_n) = f(x^*) + f'(x^*)e_n + \frac{1}{2}f''(\xi_n)e_n^2 = f'(x^*)e_n + \frac{1}{2}f''(\xi_n)e_n^2f(xn​)=f(x∗)+f′(x∗)en​+21​f′′(ξn​)en2​=f′(x∗)en​+21​f′′(ξn​)en2​
(5)

for some ξn\xi_nξn​ between xnx_nxn​ and x∗x^*x∗. The Newton step:

en+1=xn+1−x∗=en−f(xn)f′(xn)=en−f′(x∗)en+12f′′(ξn)en2f′(xn).e_{n+1} = x_{n+1} - x^* = e_n - \frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)} = e_n - \frac{f'(x^*)e_n + \frac{1}{2}f''(\xi_n)e_n^2}{f'(x_n)}.en+1​=xn+1​−x∗=en​−f′(xn​)f(xn​)​=en​−f′(xn​)f′(x∗)en​+21​f′′(ξn​)en2​​.

Since f′(xn)→f′(x∗)f'(x_n) \to f'(x^*)f′(xn​)→f′(x∗) and f′(x∗)≠0f'(x^*) \neq 0f′(x∗)=0:

22.4 Newton–Raphson for Systems¶

For a system F(x)=0\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}F(x)=0 with F:Rn→Rn\mathbf{F}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^nF:Rn→Rn, Newton–Raphson generalizes by replacing the scalar derivative with the Jacobian matrix.

Definition 22.1 (Jacobian). The Jacobian of F\mathbf{F}F at x\mathbf{x}x is the n×nn\times nn×n matrix:

JF(x)=∂F∂x=(∂F1/∂x1⋯∂F1/∂xn⋮⋮∂Fn/∂x1⋯∂Fn/∂xn).J_F(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\partial\mathbf{F}}{\partial\mathbf{x}} = \begin{pmatrix}\partial F_1/\partial x_1 & \cdots & \partial F_1/\partial x_n \\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ \partial F_n/\partial x_1 & \cdots & \partial F_n/\partial x_n\end{pmatrix}.JF​(x)=∂x∂F​=⎝⎛​∂F1​/∂x1​⋮∂Fn​/∂x1​​⋯⋯​∂F1​/∂xn​⋮∂Fn​/∂xn​​⎠⎞​.
(8)

Algorithm 22.3 (Newton–Raphson, System).

Input: F:Rn→Rn\mathbf{F}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^nF:Rn→Rn; initial guess x0\mathbf{x}_0x0​; tolerance ε\varepsilonε.

  1. For n=0,1,2,…n = 0, 1, 2, \ldotsn=0,1,2,…:

    • Compute JF(xn)J_F(\mathbf{x}_n)JF​(xn​).

    • Solve the linear system JF(xn)Δx=−F(xn)J_F(\mathbf{x}_n)\Delta\mathbf{x} = -\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}_n)JF​(xn​)Δx=−F(xn​) for Δx\Delta\mathbf{x}Δx.

    • Set xn+1=xn+Δx\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n + \Delta\mathbf{x}xn+1​=xn​+Δx.

    • If ∥xn+1−xn∥<ε\|\mathbf{x}_{n+1} - \mathbf{x}_n\| < \varepsilon∥xn+1​−xn​∥<ε or ∥F(xn+1)∥<ε\|\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}_{n+1})\| < \varepsilon∥F(xn+1​)∥<ε: return xn+1\mathbf{x}_{n+1}xn+1​.

The key step is solving JFΔx=−FJ_F\Delta\mathbf{x} = -\mathbf{F}JF​Δx=−F — a linear system in Δx\Delta\mathbf{x}Δx. This is the step that uses LU decomposition (Chapter 25). In APL, it is delta_x ← ((-F_x) ⌹ J_x).

Theorem 22.3 (Quadratic Convergence — System Newton). If F\mathbf{F}F is twice continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of x∗\mathbf{x}^*x∗, JF(x∗)J_F(\mathbf{x}^*)JF​(x∗) is invertible, and x0\mathbf{x}_0x0​ is sufficiently close to x∗\mathbf{x}^*x∗, then:

∥xn+1−x∗∥≤C∥xn−x∗∥2,\|\mathbf{x}_{n+1} - \mathbf{x}^*\| \leq C\|\mathbf{x}_n - \mathbf{x}^*\|^2,∥xn+1​−x∗∥≤C∥xn​−x∗∥2,
(9)

with CCC depending on the second derivatives of F\mathbf{F}F and ∥JF(x∗)−1∥\|J_F(\mathbf{x}^*)^{-1}\|∥JF​(x∗)−1∥.

Sufficient condition for convergence (Kantorovich theorem): Let h=∥JF(x0)−1F(x0)∥⋅∥JF(x0)−1∥⋅L/2h = \|J_F(\mathbf{x}_0)^{-1}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}_0)\|\cdot\|J_F(\mathbf{x}_0)^{-1}\|\cdot L/2h=∥JF​(x0​)−1F(x0​)∥⋅∥JF​(x0​)−1∥⋅L/2 where LLL is the Lipschitz constant of JFJ_FJF​. If h≤1/2h \leq 1/2h≤1/2, Newton–Raphson converges from x0\mathbf{x}_0x0​.

22.5 Quasi-Newton Methods: Broyden’s Method¶

Newton–Raphson requires computing the Jacobian JFJ_FJF​ at each iteration — expensive when F\mathbf{F}F is costly to evaluate or when JFJ_FJF​ has no closed form. Broyden’s method maintains an approximate Jacobian BnB_nBn​ and updates it cheaply using only function evaluations.

Algorithm 22.4 (Broyden’s Method).

Input: F\mathbf{F}F; initial guess x0\mathbf{x}_0x0​; initial Jacobian approximation B0B_0B0​ (often B0=IB_0 = IB0​=I or a finite-difference Jacobian).

For n=0,1,2,…n = 0, 1, 2, \ldotsn=0,1,2,…:

  1. Solve BnΔxn=−F(xn)B_n\Delta\mathbf{x}_n = -\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}_n)Bn​Δxn​=−F(xn​); update xn+1=xn+Δxn\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n + \Delta\mathbf{x}_nxn+1​=xn​+Δxn​.

  2. Compute ΔFn=F(xn+1)−F(xn)\Delta\mathbf{F}_n = \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}) - \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}_n)ΔFn​=F(xn+1​)−F(xn​).

  3. Broyden update: Bn+1=Bn+(ΔFn−BnΔxn)Δxn′Δxn′ΔxnB_{n+1} = B_n + \frac{(\Delta\mathbf{F}_n - B_n\Delta\mathbf{x}_n)\Delta\mathbf{x}_n'}{\Delta\mathbf{x}_n'\Delta\mathbf{x}_n}Bn+1​=Bn​+Δxn′​Δxn​(ΔFn​−Bn​Δxn​)Δxn′​​.

The Broyden update is the rank-1 correction that enforces the secant condition Bn+1Δxn=ΔFnB_{n+1}\Delta\mathbf{x}_n = \Delta\mathbf{F}_nBn+1​Δxn​=ΔFn​, while changing BnB_nBn​ as little as possible (in Frobenius norm). This generalizes the scalar secant method to systems.

Convergence: Broyden’s method achieves superlinear convergence — faster than linear but slower than quadratic. It requires only one function evaluation per iteration (vs. n+1n+1n+1 for finite-difference Jacobian Newton), making it much faster per iteration for large systems.

22.6 Worked Example: Steady State of a Medium-Scale NK Model¶

Cross-reference: Principles Ch. 23 (NK steady state) [P:Ch.23]

A medium-scale NK model has 7 steady-state conditions in 7 unknowns (C∗,K∗,Y∗,w∗,r∗,π∗,mc∗)(C^*, K^*, Y^*, w^*, r^*, \pi^*, mc^*)(C∗,K∗,Y∗,w∗,r∗,π∗,mc∗):

F(x)=(C∗−(1−sK)Y∗K∗−sKY∗/δY∗−K∗αn∗1−αw∗−(1−α)Y∗/n∗r∗−αY∗/K∗−(1−δ)π∗−πˉmc∗−w∗/[(1−α)Y∗/n∗])=0\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{pmatrix} C^* - (1-s_K)Y^* \\ K^* - s_K Y^* / \delta \\ Y^* - K^{*\alpha}n^{*1-\alpha} \\ w^* - (1-\alpha)Y^*/n^* \\ r^* - \alpha Y^*/K^* - (1-\delta) \\ \pi^* - \bar\pi \\ mc^* - w^*/[(1-\alpha)Y^*/n^*] \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{0}F(x)=⎝⎛​C∗−(1−sK​)Y∗K∗−sK​Y∗/δY∗−K∗αn∗1−αw∗−(1−α)Y∗/n∗r∗−αY∗/K∗−(1−δ)π∗−πˉmc∗−w∗/[(1−α)Y∗/n∗]​⎠⎞​=0
(10)

plus optimality conditions from household and price-setting behavior. Newton–Raphson solves this in 3–5 iterations from a reasonable starting point.

Python¶

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import fsolve

# Medium-scale NK steady state
alpha, delta, beta, theta_p = 0.36, 0.025, 0.99, 0.75
pi_bar, phi_pi, phi_y = 1.005, 1.5, 0.5  # gross inflation target

def nk_steady_state(x):
    C, K, Y, w, r, pi, mc = x
    n = 1/3  # fixed labor (for simplicity)
    
    F = np.zeros(7)
    F[0] = Y - K**alpha * n**(1-alpha)              # production
    F[1] = 1 - beta*(1+r)                            # Euler equation (r* = 1/β - 1)
    F[2] = r - (alpha*Y/K - delta)                   # MPK = r + δ
    F[3] = w - (1-alpha)*Y/n                         # MPL = w
    F[4] = mc - w/((1-alpha)*Y/n)                    # MC = w/MPL
    F[5] = pi - pi_bar                               # inflation target
    F[6] = C - (Y - delta*K)                         # goods market clearing
    return F

# Initial guess from approximate values
r_star = 1/beta - 1
K_star_approx = (alpha/(r_star+delta))**(1/(1-alpha)) * (1/3)**(1-alpha/(1-alpha))
x0 = [0.7, K_star_approx, 1.0, 2.0, r_star, pi_bar, 1.0]

x_star = fsolve(nk_steady_state, x0, full_output=False)
C_star, K_star, Y_star, w_star, r_star_sol, pi_star, mc_star = x_star
print(f"Steady state:")
print(f"  Y* = {Y_star:.4f}, K* = {K_star:.4f}, C* = {C_star:.4f}")
print(f"  r* = {r_star_sol*100:.2f}% (quarterly), mc* = {mc_star:.4f}")
print(f"  Residuals: {np.max(np.abs(nk_steady_state(x_star))):.2e}")

# Newton-Raphson from scratch (educational)
def newton_system(F, x0, tol=1e-12, max_iter=50):
    x = np.array(x0, dtype=float)
    for i in range(max_iter):
        Fx = F(x)
        if np.max(np.abs(Fx)) < tol: return x, i
        # Finite-difference Jacobian
        h = 1e-7
        J = np.zeros((len(x), len(x)))
        for j in range(len(x)):
            xp = x.copy(); xp[j] += h
            J[:,j] = (np.array(F(xp)) - Fx) / h
        dx = np.linalg.solve(J, -Fx)
        x = x + dx
    return x, max_iter

x_nr, iters = newton_system(nk_steady_state, x0)
print(f"\nNewton-Raphson converged in {iters} iterations")
print(f"Max residual: {np.max(np.abs(nk_steady_state(x_nr))):.2e}")

Julia¶

using NLsolve, LinearAlgebra

alpha, delta, beta = 0.36, 0.025, 0.99
pi_bar = 1.005; n = 1/3

function nk_ss!(F, x)
    C, K, Y, w, r, pi_, mc = x
    F[1] = Y - K^alpha * n^(1-alpha)
    F[2] = 1 - beta*(1+r)
    F[3] = r - (alpha*Y/K - delta)
    F[4] = w - (1-alpha)*Y/n
    F[5] = mc - w/((1-alpha)*Y/n)
    F[6] = pi_ - pi_bar
    F[7] = C - (Y - delta*K)
end

r_app = 1/beta - 1
K_app = (alpha/(r_app+delta))^(1/(1-alpha))*(n)^((1-alpha)/(1-alpha))
x0 = [0.7, K_app, 1.0, 2.0, r_app, pi_bar, 1.0]

sol = nlsolve(nk_ss!, x0, method=:newton, ftol=1e-12)
println("Converged: $(sol.f_converged), iterations: $(sol.iterations)")
println("Y*=$(round(sol.zero[3],digits=4)), K*=$(round(sol.zero[2],digits=4))")
library(nleqslv)

alpha<-0.36; delta<-0.025; beta<-0.99; n<-1/3; pi_bar<-1.005

nk_ss <- function(x) {
  C<-x[1]; K<-x[2]; Y<-x[3]; w<-x[4]; r<-x[5]; pi_<-x[6]; mc<-x[7]
  c(Y - K^alpha*n^(1-alpha), 1 - beta*(1+r), r-(alpha*Y/K-delta),
    w-(1-alpha)*Y/n, mc-w/((1-alpha)*Y/n), pi_-pi_bar, C-(Y-delta*K))
}

r_app<-1/beta-1; K_app<-(alpha/(r_app+delta))^(1/(1-alpha))
x0<-c(0.7, K_app, 1.0, 2.0, r_app, pi_bar, 1.0)
sol<-nleqslv(x0, nk_ss, method="Newton")
cat(sprintf("Y*=%.4f, K*=%.4f, residual=%.2e\n",sol$x[3],sol$x[2],max(abs(sol$fvec))))

22.7 Programming Exercises¶

Exercise 22.1 (APL — Broyden’s Method)¶

Implement Broyden’s method in APL as a dfn broyden ← {F B0 x0 ← ⍵ ⋄ ...}. The update step uses the rank-1 formula: B ← B + ((dF - B+.×dx) ∘.× dx) ÷ dx+.×dx. Test on the 2-equation Solow/RCK system and compare iteration counts to Newton–Raphson. Show that Broyden requires fewer function evaluations per solution.

Exercise 22.3 (Julia — Ill-Conditioning)¶

# Effect of ill-conditioning on Newton convergence
using LinearAlgebra

function ill_conditioned_system(x, kappa=1000.0)
    # Near-singular system: condition number ≈ kappa
    A = [1.0 1.0; 1.0 1.0+1/kappa]
    b = [2.0, 2.0+1/kappa]
    A*x - b  # F(x) = Ax - b, solution x* = [1, 1]
end

for kappa in [1, 10, 100, 1000, 1e6]
    F!(f,x) = (f .= ill_conditioned_system(x, kappa))
    sol = nlsolve(F!, [0.5, 0.5], method=:newton)
    cond_J = cond([1.0 1.0; 1.0 1.0+1/kappa])
    println("κ=$(kappa): cond(J)=$(round(cond_J,digits=1)), " *
            "iters=$(sol.iterations), max_err=$(round(maximum(abs.(sol.zero .- 1)),digits=8))")
end

Exercise 22.4 — RCK Steady State (⋆\star⋆)¶

The RCK model steady state satisfies: (1) f′(k∗)=δ+ρ+σgf'(k^*) = \delta + \rho + \sigma gf′(k∗)=δ+ρ+σg; (2) c∗=f(k∗)−(n+g+δ)k∗c^* = f(k^*) - (n+g+\delta)k^*c∗=f(k∗)−(n+g+δ)k∗. With f(k)=kαf(k) = k^\alphaf(k)=kα these have analytical solutions. Now use f(k)=[γkρ+(1−γ)]1/ρf(k) = [\gamma k^\rho + (1-\gamma)]^{1/\rho}f(k)=[γkρ+(1−γ)]1/ρ (CES). (a) Write the two conditions as a 2×22\times22×2 system F(k∗,c∗)=0\mathbf{F}(k^*, c^*) = \mathbf{0}F(k∗,c∗)=0. (b) Apply Newton–Raphson with finite-difference Jacobian. (c) Compare the CES steady state to the Cobb–Douglas approximation for ρ∈{−0.5,−0.1,0,0.1,0.5}\rho \in \{-0.5, -0.1, 0, 0.1, 0.5\}ρ∈{−0.5,−0.1,0,0.1,0.5}.

22.8 Chapter Summary¶

Key results:

  • Bisection: guaranteed convergence at linear rate 1/21/21/2; needs n≈3.3log⁡10(1/ε)n \approx 3.3\log_{10}(1/\varepsilon)n≈3.3log10​(1/ε) iterations; requires a bracket [a,b][a,b][a,b] with f(a)f(b)<0f(a)f(b)<0f(a)f(b)<0.

  • Newton–Raphson (scalar): xn+1=xn−f(xn)/f′(xn)x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n)xn+1​=xn​−f(xn​)/f′(xn​); quadratic convergence proved in Theorem 22.2; error satisfies ∣en+1∣≤C∣en∣2|e_{n+1}| \leq C|e_n|^2∣en+1​∣≤C∣en​∣2 near x∗x^*x∗.

  • Newton–Raphson (system): solve JF(xn)Δx=−F(xn)J_F(\mathbf{x}_n)\Delta\mathbf{x} = -\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}_n)JF​(xn​)Δx=−F(xn​) at each step via LU; quadratic convergence (Theorem 22.3); Kantorovich theorem gives sufficient conditions.

  • Broyden’s method: rank-1 Jacobian update Bn+1=Bn+(ΔF−BnΔx)Δx′/(Δx′Δx)B_{n+1} = B_n + (\Delta\mathbf{F} - B_n\Delta\mathbf{x})\Delta\mathbf{x}'/(\Delta\mathbf{x}'\Delta\mathbf{x})Bn+1​=Bn​+(ΔF−Bn​Δx)Δx′/(Δx′Δx); superlinear convergence; one function evaluation per iteration.

  • In APL: Newton–Raphson is {⍵ - (f ⍵) ÷ df ⍵}⍣≡; the system version is {x - ((-F_x) ⌹ J_x)}⍣≡.
